## Lecture Plan

- **Testing Restrictions.** Asking about several coefficients at once, and why that is not the same as asking about each.
- **Choosing a Specification.** What adjusted $R^2$ charges for a variable, and what searching across specifications costs.
- **Multicollinearity.** What correlated regressors do to a standard error, and what they leave completely alone.

::: {.tablenotes}
Reading: [chapter], and @leamer1983con, which is eleven pages, forty years old

# Testing Restrictions

## Why Separate T-Tests Cannot Answer a Joint Question

**The goal of this section:** ask a question about several coefficients at
once, and see why the answer is not the separate answers collected together.

Two situations, and the t-statistics you already have settle neither:

1. Region belongs in the equation as a **block** or not at all. Four dummies
   give you four answers and no verdict.
2. Two coefficients, each unimpressive on its own, where dropping either one
   makes the other significant.

::: {.caveat}
Four tests at the five per cent level is not a five per cent test of the four
together. Each test gets its own chance to reject, and those chances
accumulate. Hold on to that sentence: the middle section of today is the same
arithmetic, run deliberately.
:::

<!-- IDEA 1. 10-35 min. -->

## Restricted and Unrestricted Fits of the Same Model

A joint hypothesis is a claim that several coefficients are zero at the same
time. Impose it and you are simply fitting a smaller equation. So fit both.

- The **unrestricted** fit: everything in.
- The **restricted** fit: the coefficients under test set to zero, everything
  else re-estimated around them.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The same 120 people fitted twice. The
restricted fit leaves more unexplained, and the difference between the two
residual sums of squares is what the restriction cost.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-3_restricted-unrestricted: two panels sharing a y-axis. Left,
     the unrestricted fit with residual segments drawn; right, the restricted
     fit with the region dummies forced to zero and its residual segments
     drawn. Underneath, two bars giving RSS_u and RSS_r on a common scale,
     with the gap between them shaded and labelled. The point to see is that
     the gap is small, not that it exists. Needs: the same sample and the
     same vertical scale in both panels, or the comparison is theatre. -->

## Defining the F-Statistic From Two Residual Sums of Squares

**What the next equation answers:** how much fit did the restriction cost, per
restriction, measured against how much is left unexplained anyway?

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
F = \frac{\left( \mathrm{RSS}_r - \mathrm{RSS}_u \right) / q}
         {\mathrm{RSS}_u / (n - k - 1)}
\end{equation}
```

- $\mathrm{RSS}_r$: residual sum of squares from the restricted fit
- $\mathrm{RSS}_u$: residual sum of squares from the unrestricted fit
- $q$: how many coefficients the restriction sets to zero
- $n$: the number of people in the sample
- $k$: the number of slopes in the unrestricted fit

::: {.result}
$\mathrm{RSS}_r$ can never be smaller than $\mathrm{RSS}_u$, for exactly the
reason $R^2$ could not fall in 2.2. So the numerator is never negative, and
the only question is whether the fit you gave up is more than chance would
have taken from you.
:::

## Joint Confidence Regions Versus Separate Intervals

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Two coefficients at once. Each interval
on its own axis contains zero. The region that treats them jointly does not.}
```

::: {.takeaway}
Nothing here is contradictory. The separate intervals answer separate
questions, one coefficient at a time. The joint region answers the question
you actually asked, which was about both.
:::

# Choosing a Specification

## Why R-Squared Cannot Choose Between Specifications

**The goal of this section:** choose between specifications, and be honest
about what the choosing costs.

In 2.2 you voted on whether adding height in centimetres could lower $R^2$. It
cannot. Which means a rule that picks the specification with the highest $R^2$
picks the largest specification, every time, on every dataset, forever.

::: {.tablenotes}
That is not a subtle flaw. It is the selection rule refusing to select.
:::

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. -->

## Adjusted R-Squared and Its Degrees-of-Freedom Penalty

**What the next equation answers:** how well does this specification fit, per
degree of freedom it spent getting there?

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{RSS} / (n - k - 1)}
                     {\mathrm{TSS} / (n - 1)}
\end{equation}
```

- $\mathrm{RSS}$: residual sum of squares
- $\mathrm{TSS}$: total sum of squares
- $n$: the number of people in the sample
- $k$: the number of slopes in this specification

::: {.caveat title="What the penalty is worth"}
It can fall, which is the point of it, and it can go negative, which is
occasionally instructive. What it cannot do is decide for you. Adding one
variable raises $\bar{R}^2$ whenever that variable's t-statistic exceeds one
in absolute value, and one is not a standard of evidence anybody would defend
out loud.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
The statistic is Theil's [-@theil1961economic], and it was built to compare
forecasting equations, not to license a specification.
:::

## The Smallest P-Value Across Twenty Specifications

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Twenty specifications fitted to an
outcome with no signal in it, the smallest p-value kept, and the whole
exercise repeated a thousand times. The dashed line is 0.05.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
@freedman1983note made the point with pure noise: screen enough regressors on
data with nothing in it and the surviving equation looks entirely
presentable. The arithmetic is correct throughout. What is wrong is the
sentence attached to it.
:::

## Why P-Values Do Not Account for Specification Search

::: {.caveat}
A p-value of 0.04 says something about a test chosen before the data were
seen. If you fitted twenty specifications and reported the one that came in
under five per cent, the number on your slide is not that p-value, and there
is no correction printed anywhere in the output that repairs it.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Economics has measured this. @brodeur2016star and @brodeur2020methods find
published test statistics bunching just past the conventional thresholds, in
quantities no honest distribution would put there. @simmons2011false show how
few choices it takes; @gelman2014garden makes the harder version, that the
search can happen without you ever feeling that you searched.
:::

## Research Practices That Make the Search Visible

- **Say what you will do before you look.** A pre-analysis plan fixes the
  specification and the outcome in advance [@olken2015promises].
- **Report the specifications you ran, not the one that worked.** Show the
  whole set and let the reader see the spread [@simonsohn2020specification].
- **Publish the code and the data,** so the search is visible to somebody who
  did not run it [@christensen2018transparency].

::: {.caveat title="Not a rule against looking"}
Pre-specification costs something real, and nobody serious pretends otherwise
-- it forecloses things you would have learned by looking [@coffman2015pre].
Exploring is not dishonest. Exploring and then reporting it as confirmation
is. A results table with exactly one column is a claim that exactly one
specification was ever fitted, and you are entitled to ask whether that is
true.
:::

You add a variable. Schooling's coefficient barely moves, $\bar{R}^2$ rises by
0.004, and the new variable's t-statistic is 1.2.

::: {.tablenotes}

depending on whether you decided to add it before or after seeing the output?
:::

# Multicollinearity

## Two Regressors Carrying Nearly the Same Information

**The goal of this section:** say precisely what correlated regressors do to
an estimate, and then resist the reaction almost everybody has.

Schooling and years of potential experience move together in this population.
Put both in and least squares has to work out which of them is moving
earnings, using only the part of each that the other cannot account for --
the partialling out from 3.1. When that leftover part is small, there is very
little left to learn from.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The correlation between two regressors
raised from nought to 0.98. The standard error on the coefficient of interest
climbs; the fitted line and $R^2$ barely move.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-3_collinear-se: x-axis the correlation between the two
     regressors, from 0 to 0.98. Two panels sharing that axis. Top, the
     standard error on the coefficient of interest, rising steeply at the
     right-hand end. Bottom, R-squared and the point estimate, both close to
     flat, with the estimate's confidence band widening around an unmoving
     centre. Needs: the same true coefficient throughout, stated in the
     caption, so that the flat centre line reads as unbiasedness rather than
     as an accident. -->

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. -->

## Collinearity Widens Standard Errors Without Breaking Assumptions

::: {.result}
Collinearity breaks no assumption. The estimates are still unbiased, the
fitted values and $R^2$ are hardly touched, Gauss-Markov still holds, and the
standard errors are still right. They are simply large -- because the data
genuinely cannot separate two things that move together.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
@goldberger1991course made the point by inventing a matching disease,
*micronumerosity*, meaning not enough observations, and giving it the same
solemn treatment textbooks give collinearity. Both are statements that your
sample carries less information than you wanted. Nobody writes a diagnostics
section about having a small sample.
:::

## Why Dropping a Collinear Regressor Introduces Bias

::: {.caveat}
The instinct is to drop one of the two. That does narrow the standard error,
and it narrows it by declining to answer the question: the surviving
coefficient now carries the omitted variable bias of 3.1, and it is no longer
the partial effect you set out to estimate. You have traded a wide interval
for a narrow one in the wrong place.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
@lindner2020misconceptions trace how routinely this is done in published work,
and what it does to the estimates. @vanhove2021collinearity works through the
rest of the standard remedies and finds each of them quietly answering a
different question from the one that was asked.
:::

## Variance Inflation Factors and Their Conventional Thresholds

- A variance inflation factor says how much wider a standard error is than it
  would be if that regressor were uncorrelated with the others. A real
  quantity, and worth looking at.
- The thresholds -- five, ten -- are conventions, not results. Whether an
  inflated standard error is a problem depends on whether the interval is
  still narrow enough to answer your question [@obrien2007caution].
- What actually helps is what helped in 2.3: more people, or more spread in
  the regressor you care about.

::: {.takeaway}
Collinearity is a fact about your data, not a fault in your model. The
regression is not misbehaving. It is reporting what it does not know.
:::

## Vote: Is This a Collinearity Problem?

Schooling and experience correlate at 0.85. Schooling's coefficient is 1.4
with a standard error of 0.9, and $R^2$ is 0.31.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what would you have to
change about the data, rather than about the model, to narrow that interval?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: this is the only specification we fitted, and we chose
it before we saw the estimate. Every claim the p-value makes rests on that,
and nothing in the table can tell you whether it is so.]

Search on purpose, on data you know has nothing in it.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote first: out of twenty specifications fitted to an outcome with no signal,

:::

## Summary: Joint Tests, Model Choice and Collinearity

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Testing Restrictions.** An F-test compares a restricted fit against an unrestricted one, and answers a question the separate t-tests cannot.
2. **Choosing a Specification.** Adjusted R-squared charges for a variable, but no fit statistic charges for the search that found the specification.
3. **Multicollinearity.** Correlated regressors widen standard errors and break nothing, and dropping one buys its precision with bias.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Next week: the Gauss-Markov assumptions from 2.3, and how you would notice one
of them failing in data you did not simulate yourself.
:::

## Derivation: The F-Statistic as Restricted Against Unrestricted Fit

Fit the equation twice, once with the restriction imposed and once without,
and write the cost of the restriction as a ratio of two separate estimates of
the same error variance.

::: {.tablenotes}
Four steps. Write the restricted equation as the unrestricted one with $q$
coefficients set to zero; show that the restricted residual sum of squares
cannot be the smaller of the two; divide the difference by $q$ and the
unrestricted residual sum of squares by $n - k - 1$; show that under the null
both of those are estimating the same error variance, so their ratio follows
an $F$ distribution with $q$ and $n - k - 1$ degrees of freedom. The step that
does the work is the last one, and it is the step that needs the assumptions
of 2.3 and normal errors on top of them.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

## Derivation: When Adjusted R-Squared Rises

Show that adding one variable raises $\bar{R}^2$ if and only if that
variable's t-statistic is greater than one in absolute value.

::: {.tablenotes}
Two steps and no new machinery. Write $\bar{R}^2$ for the small and the large
equation in terms of their residual sums of squares, take the difference, and
recognise what is left as the square of a t-statistic compared with one. The
result is the justification for the caveat in section two: the threshold
$\bar{R}^2$ imposes is real, and it is far below anything you would call
evidence.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]
